hard_constraints: Ronnie never confesses on purpose. The truth only ever gets closer by accident.
Present day. No ten-shilling notes, no shillings, no Austin Cambridges, no coronation mints. If it could not be bought on Bellamy Road this month, it is not in shot.

style_notes.text: Dry English deadpan. Nobody in this show knows they are in a comedy. The laughs come from people being sincere at exactly the wrong moment.
Small concrete objects over jokes: fibreglass, a biscuit tin of raffle money, a laminated timetable, a folding chair. Never let a character knowingly deliver a punchline.
Ronnie lies fluently and then badly, in that order: the first lie is smooth, and the one he adds five seconds later is much worse and he cannot take it back.
At most one simile per paragraph, and never a simile about a smile. Deadpan means the narration does not perform. Dialogue does the work.
Limit descriptive detail to essential elements
Keep dialogue direct and to the point

criteria.name: escalating cost
criteria.description: Each near-miss must force Ronnie into a NEW lie that costs him more than the last one - more money, more labour, or more of somebody trusting him. If the situation resets to neutral, or the lie costs nothing, score it low.

criteria.name: near-exposure on screen
criteria.description: The cast itself must nearly be discovered in front of a witness, physically and in public - seen, touched, cut into, or forced to bear weight. Characters discussing the risk does not count. The leg has to almost give the game away.

criteria.name: compulsory hook
criteria.description: The last beat must leave a specific, dated, unavoidable obligation on Ronnie that makes the next episode inevitable - a booked appointment, a public event, a person arriving. Vague unease is not a hook.

rejected_directions: The near-miss is defused by talking, not by his body. A physiotherapist does not carry a portable ultrasound to a bus stop, so the threat is a prop rather than a person, and paying for folding chairs is a cost with no comic ladder in it - it does not force a bigger lie next week.

Ronnie is inventing baroque nonsense (air channels, a consultant in Zurich) instead of panicking. He should be a bad liar under pressure, not a fantasist with a plan. Also nobody sincere is hurt here, and sincerity being wasted on him is where the comedy lives.

Inventing a second injury is the laziest available escalation - it costs him nothing but more of the same lie. Forty pounds for a folding chair is not a debt anybody can build an episode on. I want the escalation to be labour or public obligation he physically cannot fake his way out of.

This was ranked top and it destroys the series. If Marguerite watches Ronnie stride away with the crutches under his arm, she knows - and the whole show is her believing him. Making her a knowing accomplice removes the only sincere person in it. Never let a character who is being conned see the con work.

The community centre electricity being cut off is a different, sadder show. Ronnie should be spending the money on nothing memorable - debts, a butcher bill - not on a hardship that makes us feel sorry for him. Sympathy for Ronnie is poison this early.
Hauling folding chairs up the stairs right now is a chore, not an escalation - it is over by the end of the scene and costs him nothing next week. The lie has to buy him a debt with a date on it.

Second time the generator has had a witness see the con work - I rejected exactly this at scene level (Marguerite watching from the post office) and gave the reason. Arthur seeing the crutches go under the arm ends the series in the cold open. Nobody watches Ronnie when he is alone.

This is the parent scene summary handed back to me as a beat. Three of the six did the same thing - same sentences, same order, nothing decomposed. A beat should be one action inside the scene, not a restatement of it.

Four pounds ten. I put a present-day hard constraint in the ledger two hours ago and this is still pricing things in pre-decimal money, same as the ten-shilling note and the Austin Cambridge earlier. Also four pounds is not a cost - the whole point is the lie has to hurt his pocket.

This is scene one again - another supervision session with another invented Zurich rule - and it was ranked top. I asked for the closing scene of the episode and got a repeat of its opening. Nothing here is a hook: a lumbar puncture next Tuesday is not a reason to watch episode three.
